decks.title: The Mauryan Empire — Part 1: Sources, Rulers and Administration
goals: Name the authors of the Arthashastra and the Indika and state what each tells us
Explain the importance of the Ashokan Edicts and the Sanchi Stupa as sources
List the major Mauryan rulers in chronological order with approximate reigns
Describe central, provincial and city administration, including Pataliputra

slides.heading: The Mauryan Empire: sources, rulers and administration
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about the Mauryas, who ruled, and how the empire was governed.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the sources of Mauryan history, the three rulers in order, and how the empire was governed
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we learn how historians know about the Mauryan Empire. We meet its three great rulers in order, and then see how the king, his ministers, governors and city officials ran so large an empire.

slides.heading: Four sources at a glance

rows: Treatise on statecraft, attributed to Kautilya
How a state was expected to be run
Account by the Greek envoy Megasthenes
Pataliputra and the court, seen by a foreigner
Royal messages carved on rocks and pillars
Ashoka's Dhamma and policies, in his own words

visual.alt: Table of four sources: the Arthashastra is a treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya, the Indika an account by Megasthenes, the Ashokan Edicts are carved royal messages, and Sanchi Stupa is a Buddhist monument in Madhya Pradesh

slides.narration: Four sources help us to study the Mauryas. The Arthashastra is a treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya. The Indika is an account by the Greek envoy Megasthenes. The Ashokan Edicts are royal messages carved on rocks and pillars. The Sanchi Stupa is a Buddhist monument in Madhya Pradesh.

slides.heading: The Arthashastra
bullets: Attributed to **Kautilya**, also called **Chanakya**, minister of Chandragupta.
A **treatise on statecraft**: revenue, spies, war and justice.
Its **date is debated** and some parts may be **later**.
Read it **with care** and **with other sources**.

rows: Attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), minister of Chandragupta
Revenue, spies, war, justice, the duties of a king
Its date is debated; some parts may be later

visual.alt: Table about the Arthashastra: attributed to Kautilya or Chanakya, a treatise on statecraft covering revenue, spies, war and justice, with the caution that its date is debated and some parts may be later

slides.narration: The Arthashastra is traditionally attributed to Kautilya, also called Chanakya, a minister of Chandragupta. It is a treatise on how a state should be run, covering revenue, spies, war and justice. Scholars debate its date, and some parts may be later, so historians read it with care and together with other sources.

slides.heading: The Indika of Megasthenes
bullets: Written by **Megasthenes**, envoy of **Seleucus Nikator** at **Pataliputra**.
Describes the **city, the court and society** as a foreigner saw them.
It **survives only through quotations** by later Greek and Roman writers.

nodes.label: Seleucus Nikator sends Megasthenes as envoy
He observes Pataliputra and the court
His Indika survives only in quotations by later writers

visual.alt: Flow: Seleucus Nikator sends Megasthenes as envoy, he observes Pataliputra and the court, and his Indika survives only in quotations by later Greek and Roman writers
visual.caption: The Indika: how it reached us.

slides.narration: Megasthenes was sent as an envoy by Seleucus Nikator to the court of Chandragupta at Pataliputra. His book, the Indika, describes the city, the court and society as a foreigner saw them. The original is lost, and we know it only from quotations by later Greek and Roman writers.

slides.heading: The Ashokan Edicts
bullets: Messages carved on **rocks and pillars** across the empire.
Mostly **Prakrit** in **Brahmi**; other scripts in the north-west.
**Deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.**
They record **Dhamma**, the **Kalinga War** and **welfare**.

rows: Rocks and pillars across the empire
Mostly Prakrit in Brahmi; Kharosthi in the north-west; Greek and Aramaic in the far north-west
Dhamma, the Kalinga War, welfare measures

visual.alt: Table about the Ashokan Edicts: carved on rocks and pillars, mostly Prakrit in Brahmi script with Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic in the north-west, deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, and recording Dhamma, the Kalinga War and welfare

slides.narration: The Ashokan Edicts are messages carved on rocks and pillars across the empire. Most are in the Prakrit language in the Brahmi script, with other languages in the north-west. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in eighteen thirty seven. The edicts record Ashoka's Dhamma, the Kalinga War and his welfare measures in his own words.

slides.narration: This is a schematic map, not drawn to scale. It shows some places linked with the Mauryas. Pataliputra was the capital. Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri were provincial capitals. Sarnath and Sanchi are famous for their monuments. Edicts were set up in many regions, so that people everywhere could see them.

slides.heading: The Sanchi Stupa
bullets: A **Buddhist monument** in **Madhya Pradesh**.
**Begun under Ashoka** and **enlarged later**.
The **carved gateways** were added about the **first century BCE**.
Evidence of **Buddhist art, belief and royal patronage**.

rows: Carved gateways added about the first century BCE
Shows Buddhist art, belief and royal patronage

visual.alt: Table about Sanchi Stupa: in Madhya Pradesh, begun under Ashoka and enlarged later, carved gateways added about the first century BCE, and valuable as evidence of Buddhist art, belief and royal patronage

slides.narration: The Sanchi Stupa stands in Madhya Pradesh. It was begun under Ashoka and enlarged later, and its carved gateways were added about the first century before the common era. It is a useful source because its carvings show Buddhist art and belief, and its beginning shows royal support for Buddhism.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the right source
slides.body_md: Ask what you want to know, then pick the source that fits.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the question the historian is asking.
Step 2 — Decide: statecraft, a foreign view, the ruler's own words, or art?
Step 3 — Match it with the right source.
Step 4 — Add a caution about that kind of source.

rows: How did the Mauryas expect a king to run revenue and spies?
What did a foreign envoy notice about Pataliputra?
What did Ashoka say about the Kalinga War?
What art did Buddhists create in this age?

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Read the question and decide whether it is about statecraft, a foreign view, the ruler's own words or art. Then match it with the right source. Statecraft goes to the Arthashastra. A foreign view goes to the Indika. The ruler's own words are in the edicts. Art is at Sanchi. Finally, add a caution suited to that source.

slides.narration: The three major Mauryan rulers were Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara and Ashoka. The boxes are drawn roughly to scale. Chandragupta ruled from about three hundred twenty one before the common era, Bindusara from about two hundred ninety seven, and Ashoka from about two hundred sixty eight. Books differ a little, so say about.

slides.heading: Chandragupta Maurya
bullets: **Overthrew the Nandas** and founded the empire.
Fought **Seleucus Nikator**; a **treaty** ended the conflict.
The treaty left the north-west **secure**.
**Megasthenes** then came to **Pataliputra** as envoy.

nodes.label: Conflict with Seleucus, treaty about 305 to 303 BCE

visual.alt: Flow: Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas about 321 BCE, fought Seleucus and made a treaty about 305 to 303 BCE, and Megasthenes came to Pataliputra as envoy
visual.caption: Chandragupta Maurya, in order.

slides.narration: Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas and founded the Mauryan Empire in about three hundred twenty one before the common era. In the north-west he fought Seleucus Nikator, and a treaty ended the conflict. After it, Megasthenes came to Pataliputra as an envoy. The treaty left the frontier secure and brought the Mauryas recognition abroad.

slides.heading: Bindusara and Ashoka

rows: Founder; overthrew the Nandas; treaty with Seleucus
Son of Chandragupta; held the empire together

visual.alt: Table of the three rulers with approximate reigns and what each is commonly taught for: Chandragupta the founder, Bindusara son of Chandragupta who held the empire together, and Ashoka for the Kalinga War, Dhamma and edicts

slides.narration: Bindusara was the son of Chandragupta and the father of Ashoka, and he held the empire together. Ashoka came after him and is remembered for the Kalinga War, for Dhamma and for his edicts. Remember the order Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka, and give each reign with the word about.

visual.caption: Mauryan administration (simplified).

slides.narration: This chart shows the administration in simple form. The king stood at the centre and was helped by a council of ministers called the mantriparishad. Below him were central officials, provinces ruled by princes called kumaras, and the capital city of Pataliputra with its own board of officials.

slides.heading: Centre and provinces
bullets: The **king** had the final authority; ministers **advised** him.
The **samaharta** handled **revenue**; the **sannidhata** the **treasury**.
Provinces were ruled by **kumaras**, with capitals such as **Taxila**, **Ujjain**, **Tosali** and **Suvarnagiri**.
Provinces had **districts** and **villages**.

rows: King, helped by the council of ministers

visual.alt: Table of three levels of government: the centre with the king and ministers, provinces under kumaras with capitals such as Taxila and Ujjain, and districts and villages under local officials

slides.narration: At the centre, the king had the final authority and a council of ministers advised him. The samaharta handled revenue and the sannidhata kept the treasury. Provinces were ruled by princes called kumaras, from capitals such as Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. Each province had districts and villages that passed orders downward.

slides.heading: Pataliputra: a city with a board
bullets: A **board of thirty**, in **six committees of five**.
Committees looked after matters such as **crafts, trade, foreigners** and **births and deaths**.
The account comes from **Megasthenes**: paraphrase and read with care.

rows: Crafts, trade, foreigners, births and deaths
A foreigner's report; read with care

visual.alt: Table about Pataliputra as reported from Megasthenes: a board of thirty members in six committees of five dealing with crafts, trade, foreigners and births and deaths, with the caution that it is a foreigner's report

slides.narration: As reported from Megasthenes, the capital Pataliputra was run by a board of thirty members, divided into six committees of five. The committees looked after matters such as crafts, trade, foreigners, and births and deaths. We repeat this in our own words and remember that it is a foreigner's report.

decks.title: The Mauryan Empire — Part 2: Ashoka's Dhamma and Its Impact
goals: Explain how the Kalinga War influenced Ashoka
Explain the principles of Dhamma: tolerance, non-violence, respect for elders and kindness to servants
Evaluate the impact of Dhamma on administration, the spread of Buddhism and culture
Present the debated view on the weakening of the empire

slides.heading: Ashoka's Dhamma and its impact
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a war, a change of heart, and what followed.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the Kalinga War, the principles of Dhamma, and the impact of Dhamma
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we study the Kalinga War and how it changed Ashoka. We then learn the principles of his Dhamma and weigh its impact on administration, on Buddhism and on Indian culture. We also see why some historians debate its effects.

slides.heading: The Kalinga War
bullets: Fought in about **261 BCE**.
The edicts describe great **suffering**.
Ashoka expressed **remorse**.
He set aside **conquest by war**.

nodes.label: Great suffering; Ashoka's remorse recorded in the edicts
Conquest by war set aside; Dhamma promoted

visual.alt: Flow: the Kalinga War about 261 BCE caused great suffering, the edicts record Ashoka's remorse, and he set aside conquest by war and promoted Dhamma
visual.caption: From the Kalinga War to Dhamma.

slides.narration: The Kalinga War was fought in about two hundred sixty one before the common era. The edicts describe the great suffering it caused, and they record that Ashoka felt sorrow. After this, he set aside conquest by war and turned to Dhamma. We give no figures, only what the edicts say.

slides.heading: Quick check: a turning point
slides.body_md: Which statement best describes the change in Ashoka's policy?
slides.narration: Think about what the edicts say about his feelings after the war, and which policy he promoted afterwards.

slides.heading: Principles of Dhamma
bullets: **Tolerance** of all sects.
**Non-violence** towards people and animals.
**Respect** for elders and teachers.
**Kindness** to servants.

rows: Respect for the beliefs of others
Avoiding needless harm to people and animals
Fair and gentle treatment of those who work for us

visual.alt: Table of four principles of Dhamma: tolerance of all sects, non-violence, respect for elders and teachers, and kindness to servants

slides.narration: Ashoka's Dhamma had several principles. Tolerance meant respect for the beliefs of all sects. Non-violence meant avoiding needless harm to people and animals. People were to respect their elders and teachers, and to be kind to servants. The care of people and animals was also taught.

slides.heading: What kind of thing was Dhamma?
slides.body_md: Many historians describe Dhamma as a **moral code**, not a separate religion.

rows: A moral code for people of all sects
A separate new religion, in the view of many historians
A tax or a military order

visual.alt: Table: Dhamma was a moral code for people of all sects, announced in public edicts and linked to welfare; it was not, in the view of many historians, a separate new religion, nor forced on people, nor a tax or military order

slides.narration: What was Dhamma? Many historians describe it as a moral code for people of all sects, and not as a separate new religion. It was announced in public edicts and it was linked to welfare. It was not forced on people, and it was not a tax or a military order.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: sorting actions into principles
slides.body_md: Match each imagined action to a principle, then give the reason.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the action.
Step 2 — Ask who is being treated well: a different faith, an animal, a worker.
Step 3 — Name the principle.
Step 4 — Write the reason in one line.

rows: Two neighbours of different faiths share a festival ground
A carter refuses to overload his bullocks
A weaver lets his helper rest after a long day

visual.alt: Table sorting three imagined actions into principles: neighbours sharing a festival ground show tolerance, a carter not overloading bullocks shows non-violence, and a weaver letting his helper rest shows kindness to servants

slides.narration: Use four steps. Read the action. Ask who is being treated well, such as a person of a different faith, an animal or a worker. Name the principle and write the reason in one line. Neighbours sharing a festival ground show tolerance. A carter who will not overload his bullocks shows non-violence. A weaver who lets his helper rest shows kindness to servants.

slides.heading: Quick check: separate religion?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about Dhamma is true or false.
slides.narration: Think about how many historians describe Dhamma, and whether it was forced on people.

slides.heading: The Dhamma-mahamattas
bullets: Special officers appointed by Ashoka.
They **travelled among the people**.
They explained **Dhamma** and looked after **welfare**.
They worked for people of **all sects**.

nodes.label: They explain Dhamma and look after welfare of all sects

visual.alt: Flow: Ashoka appoints Dhamma-mahamattas who travel among the people, explain Dhamma and look after the welfare of people of all sects
visual.caption: The work of the Dhamma-mahamattas.

slides.narration: To spread Dhamma, Ashoka appointed special officers called Dhamma-mahamattas. They travelled among the people, explained right conduct and looked after the welfare of people of all sects. This shows that Dhamma was not only a personal belief of the king, but also a public policy.

slides.heading: Welfare measures

rows: Water and rest on the road

visual.alt: Table of welfare measures: roads with shade trees for comfort, wells and rest-houses for water and rest, and care for people and animals with medical help and medicinal plants

slides.narration: The edicts record welfare measures. Roads were planted with shade trees, and wells and rest-houses were set up for travellers. There was care for people and animals, with medical help and medicinal plants. These measures are one reason why Ashoka's rule is remembered.

slides.heading: Impact on administration
bullets: **Dhamma-mahamattas** were appointed.
Officials were urged to treat people **fairly**.
**Welfare** became part of government.

nodes.label: Officials urged to treat people fairly
Welfare added to the work of government

visual.alt: Flow: Dhamma-mahamattas appointed, officials urged to treat people fairly, and welfare added to the work of government
visual.caption: Dhamma and administration.

slides.narration: Dhamma affected the administration. Dhamma-mahamattas were appointed, officials were urged to treat people fairly, and welfare became a part of the work of government. The edicts also served as public messages, carved where many people could see them.

slides.heading: The spread of Buddhism
slides.body_md: Ashoka supported Buddhism, while his Dhamma was addressed to **people of all sects**.

nodes.label: Missions abroad, including Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka

visual.alt: Flow: royal support and stupas, the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra, and missions abroad including Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka
visual.caption: How Buddhism spread.

slides.narration: Ashoka supported Buddhism. He built stupas, and the Third Buddhist Council is traditionally held at Pataliputra. Missions were sent abroad, including Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka. At the same time, his Dhamma was addressed to people of all sects, so we keep the two ideas separate.

slides.heading: Culture and legacy

visual.alt: Table of cultural legacy: stupas such as Sanchi as centres of Buddhist art, pillars with edicts as public messages in stone, and the Lion Capital of Sarnath as the source of the national emblem of India

slides.narration: Ashoka left a lasting mark on culture. Stupas such as Sanchi became centres of Buddhist art. Pillars carried public messages in stone. The Lion Capital of Sarnath, a pillar top with four lions, is the source of the national emblem of India.

slides.heading: Quick check: a pillar with four lions
slides.body_md: Which statement about the Sarnath pillar top is correct?
slides.narration: Think about the monument found at Sarnath and about what it gave to modern India.

slides.heading: Was the empire weakened?
slides.body_md: Historians **debate** the causes of the later weakening of the empire.

rows: Stress on Dhamma and non-violence reduced military strength
Weak successors and the size of the empire were the main causes
Pressure on revenue and the cost of government

visual.alt: Table of debated views on the later weakening of the empire: some historians cite reduced military strength from the stress on Dhamma, others weak successors and the size of the empire, and others pressure on revenue

slides.narration: After Ashoka, the empire weakened. Some historians link this to his policies, because a stress on Dhamma and non-violence may have reduced military strength. Others point to weak successors and the size of the empire. Others point to pressure on revenue. The causes are debated, so a careful answer gives more than one view.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: planning a 10-mark evaluation
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Administration and welfare. [3] (ii) Buddhism and culture. [3] (iii) Two views on weakening. [4]
bullets: (i) Dhamma-mahamattas; one welfare measure.
(ii) Council and missions; stupas and pillars.
(iii) One view, the other view, then why debated.
Use neutral words: some historians, others.

rows: Effect on administration; one welfare measure; Dhamma-mahamattas
Buddhism: council, missions; culture: stupas, pillars
Two views on weakening; why debated

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer on the impact of Dhamma: part (i) administration and welfare for 3 marks, part (ii) Buddhism and culture for 3 marks, part (iii) two views on weakening for 4 marks

slides.narration: Plan this answer in three parts. Part one covers administration and one welfare measure. Part two covers Buddhism, with the council and missions, and culture, with stupas and pillars. Part three gives one view on the weakening, then the other view, and ends by saying why it is debated.

slides.heading: Quick check: why Dhamma after Kalinga?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether one explains the other.
slides.narration: Check each statement on its own first. Then ask whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: The **Kalinga War**, about **261 BCE**, led to **remorse** and **Dhamma**.
Principles: **tolerance, non-violence, respect, kindness**.
**Dhamma-mahamattas** and **welfare** shaped administration.
**Buddhism** spread; **stupas** and the **Lion Capital** remain.

visual.alt: Table of cultural legacy: stupas such as Sanchi as centres of Buddhist art, pillars with edicts as public messages in stone, and the Lion Capital of Sarnath as the source of the national emblem of India

slides.narration: To sum up. The Kalinga War led Ashoka to Dhamma. Its principles were tolerance, non-violence, respect for elders and kindness to servants. Dhamma-mahamattas and welfare shaped administration, Buddhism spread, and stupas and the Lion Capital remain. The reasons for the later weakening of the empire are debated.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: Give the **date** of the Kalinga War as **about 261 BCE**; do not give casualty figures.
Name **four principles** and match them with an **example**.
Call Dhamma a **moral code for all sects**; say it was not forced.
In an evaluation, write **some historians** and **others**.
Spell the officers: **Dhamma-mahamattas**.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Give the date of the Kalinga War as about two hundred sixty one before the common era, and do not invent figures. Name four principles and match them with examples. Call Dhamma a moral code for all sects. In an evaluation, write some historians and others. And spell Dhamma-mahamattas with care.

notes.title: The Mauryan Empire — notes

sections.heading: 1. Sources of Mauryan history
sections.body_md:
- **Arthashastra:** treatise on statecraft attributed to **Kautilya** (Chanakya), minister of Chandragupta; revenue, spies, war, justice. Rediscovered and published by R. Shamasastry in the early 1900s. Its date is debated and some parts may be later: read it with care.
- **Indika:** by **Megasthenes**, Greek envoy of Seleucus Nikator at Pataliputra; describes the city, court and society as a foreigner saw them. Survives only in quotations by later Greek and Roman writers.
- **Ashokan Edicts:** carved on rocks and pillars, mostly Prakrit in Brahmi script (Kharosthi in the north-west; Greek and Aramaic in the far north-west). Deciphered by **James Prinsep in 1837**. Ashoka calls himself Devanampiya Piyadasi.
- **Sanchi Stupa:** Madhya Pradesh; begun under Ashoka, enlarged later; carved gateways added about the first century BCE.

A royal order or message, here carved in stone.

sections.heading: 3. The three rulers
sections.body_md:
- **Chandragupta Maurya** (about 321 to 297 BCE): overthrew the Nandas; conflict with Seleucus Nikator and a treaty (about 305 to 303 BCE); Megasthenes came as envoy.
- **Bindusara** (about 297 to 273 BCE): son of Chandragupta; held the empire together.
- **Ashoka** (about 268 to 232 BCE): Kalinga War, Dhamma, edicts.
- Dates are approximate and vary between books; say **about**.

sections.heading: 4. Administration
sections.body_md:
- **Centre:** the king, helped by the council of ministers (**mantriparishad**); officials such as the **samaharta** (revenue) and **sannidhata** (treasury).
- **Provinces:** ruled by princes (**kumaras**) with capitals such as Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri; divided into districts and villages.
- **Pataliputra:** as reported from Megasthenes, a board of **thirty** in **six committees of five**, dealing with matters such as crafts, trade, foreigners and births and deaths.
- **Spies** reported to the king; a large **army** defended the empire.

sections.heading: 5. Ashoka and Dhamma
sections.body_md:
- The **Kalinga War** (about **261 BCE**): the edicts describe great suffering and Ashoka's remorse; he set aside conquest by war.
- **Principles of Dhamma:** tolerance of all sects, non-violence, respect for elders and teachers, kindness to servants, welfare of people and animals.
- **Dhamma-mahamattas** were appointed to spread Dhamma and look after welfare.
- Many historians call Dhamma a **moral code for people of all sects**, not a separate new religion.

sections.heading: 6. Impact of Dhamma
sections.body_md:
- **Administration:** Dhamma-mahamattas; officials urged to treat people fairly; welfare as part of government.
- **Welfare:** roads with shade trees, wells, rest-houses, care for people and animals.
- **Buddhism:** royal support, stupas, the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra, missions (Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka).
- **Culture:** stupas such as Sanchi; pillars; the **Lion Capital of Sarnath**, the source of India's national emblem.
- **Debate:** some historians link the later weakening of the empire to Ashoka's policies; others point to weak successors, size and revenue.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about.
- Mixing up the author of the Arthashastra (Kautilya) and of the Indika (Megasthenes).
- Writing that Megasthenes was an Indian minister.
- Calling Dhamma a new religion forced on people.
- Giving casualty figures for the Kalinga War.
- Saying one cause alone destroyed the empire.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A guide in an imagined museum at Patna describes a treatise on statecraft that advises kings on revenue, spies, war and justice. Who is traditionally named as its author?

options.text_md: Kautilya, also called Chanakya, minister of Chandragupta
James Prinsep, who deciphered the Brahmi script
Ashoka, who set up the pillars

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Kautilya, also called Chanakya, minister of Chandragupta. The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya). Megasthenes wrote the Indika, James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837, and Ashoka issued the edicts; none of them wrote the Arthashastra.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined letter, a Greek envoy at Pataliputra writes that he is collecting notes on the city, its rulers and its people for readers back home. Which known work, and which author, does his task resemble?

options.text_md: The Indika by Megasthenes, envoy of Seleucus Nikator

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Indika by Megasthenes, envoy of Seleucus Nikator. Megasthenes was a Greek envoy at the court of Chandragupta who wrote the Indika. The Arthashastra is a treatise by an Indian minister, the edicts are royal messages, and Sanchi is a monument.

questions.stem_md: A guide at an imagined heritage walk says, "For centuries nobody could read the writing on the rock, until a scholar deciphered it in 1837." Why was that achievement important for the study of the Mauryas?

options.text_md: It allowed historians to read the Ashokan Edicts, which are written in Brahmi script, and learn the ruler's own words and policies
It proved that the Arthashastra was written in a single year
It showed that Megasthenes had never visited India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It allowed historians to read the Ashokan Edicts, which are written in Brahmi script, and learn the ruler's own words and policies. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837, which opened the edicts to historians. The other options have no connection with the deciphering.

questions.stem_md: An imagined guide notes that one Ashokan edict in the far north-west was carved in Greek and Aramaic, while most others use Prakrit in the Brahmi script. What can a historian infer?

options.text_md: The edicts were all written by foreigners
The ruler wished his messages to be understood by people of different languages in different regions
The edicts were meant to be read only by the king's ministers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The ruler wished his messages to be understood by people of different languages in different regions. Using the local languages and scripts of a region shows that the messages were meant for the people there. It does not show a small realm or foreign authorship, and the edicts were public, not secret.

questions.stem_md: Students visiting Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh are told by an imagined guide, "The stupa was begun in Ashoka's time, and the carved gateways were added much later." Which statement about Sanchi is correct?

options.text_md: It is a palace in which Ashoka lived
It is a city whose administration was run by a board of thirty
It is a Buddhist monument whose carvings help us learn about the religion and art of the period
It is a treatise on statecraft

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is a Buddhist monument whose carvings help us learn about the religion and art of the period. Sanchi Stupa is a Buddhist monument, and its carvings are evidence of belief and art. The palace, the city board and the treatise belong to other sources.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined history club says, "Every rule in the Arthashastra was followed exactly in Chandragupta's empire." Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: It is a treatise on how a state should be run, its date is debated and parts may be later, so it must be read with other sources
The student is right, because the book was written by the emperor himself
The student is right, because the book was found in Pataliputra in the Mauryan age
The student is wrong, because the Arthashastra says nothing about government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is a treatise on how a state should be run, its date is debated and parts may be later, so it must be read with other sources. A treatise describes what a state ought to do; scholars debate its date and some parts may be later additions. It was not written by the emperor, and it does discuss government at length.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Megasthenes, the author of the Indika, was a minister of Chandragupta who wrote in Sanskrit.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Megasthenes was a Greek envoy sent by Seleucus Nikator to the court of Chandragupta, and his work survives only through later Greek and Roman writers.

questions.stem_md: The treatise on statecraft called the Arthashastra is traditionally attributed to ___.
questions.solution_md: It is attributed to Kautilya, also called Chanakya.

questions.stem_md: The Sanchi Stupa is in the Indian state of ___.
questions.solution_md: Sanchi is in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.stem_md: Match each source of Mauryan history with what it is.

match_right.text_md: Account by the Greek envoy Megasthenes
Treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya
Royal messages carved on rocks and pillars

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The Arthashastra is a treatise by Kautilya, the Indika an account by Megasthenes, the edicts are carved royal messages, and Sanchi is a Buddhist monument.

questions.stem_md: Why are the Ashokan Edicts considered a very valuable source of Mauryan history?
questions.solution_md: Issued by the ruler; tell of Dhamma and Kalinga.

answer.model_answer_md: They were issued by **Ashoka himself** and carved on **rocks and pillars**, so they preserve his own words. They tell us about his **Dhamma**, the **Kalinga War** and his **welfare measures**.

marking_scheme.step: Issued by Ashoka himself and carved in stone
Information on Dhamma, Kalinga or welfare

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the Sanchi Stupa helps a historian of the Mauryan age.
questions.solution_md: Patronage; art and belief.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It was **begun under Ashoka**, so it shows his **patronage of Buddhism**.
2. Its **carved gateways** and railings show the **art and beliefs** of the age, including scenes from the Buddha's life.

marking_scheme.step: Carvings as evidence of art and belief

questions.stem_md: An imagined student reads a Greek writer who says he is quoting a lost account of Chandragupta's court. Name the lost work and say why a historian reads such a quotation with care.
questions.solution_md: Indika; survives in quotations; foreign observer.

answer.model_answer_md: The lost work is the **Indika** of **Megasthenes**. It survives only through **quotations** by later Greek and Roman writers, and Megasthenes was a **foreigner**, so he may have misunderstood things.

marking_scheme.step: Reason for care: only quotations survive or foreign viewpoint

questions.stem_md: Name three sources of Mauryan history and state one thing each tells us.
questions.solution_md: Three sources with contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Arthashastra** (attributed to Kautilya) tells us how a state was expected to be governed.
2. The **Indika** (Megasthenes) describes Pataliputra and the Mauryan court as seen by a foreigner.
3. The **Ashokan Edicts** record Ashoka's Dhamma and policies in his own words.

marking_scheme.step: Edicts or Sanchi and its use

questions.stem_md: On an imagined timeline game at Class IX Open Day, the card reads: "I overthrew the Nandas and founded the Mauryan Empire in about 321 BCE." Which ruler holds the card?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Chandragupta Maurya. Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas and founded the empire. Bindusara and Ashoka ruled after him, and Seleucus Nikator was a Greek ruler, not a Mauryan.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum panel reads: "A war between the Mauryan king and a Greek ruler in the north-west ended with a treaty, and an envoy then came to Pataliputra." Which pair of rulers fits the panel?

options.text_md: Bindusara and Seleucus Nikator, about 270 BCE
Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus Nikator, about 305 to 303 BCE
Ashoka and the rulers of Kalinga, about 261 BCE
Chandragupta Maurya and the Nandas, about 321 BCE

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus Nikator, about 305 to 303 BCE. The conflict and treaty with Seleucus, followed by the arrival of Megasthenes as envoy, belong to Chandragupta's reign. Kalinga and the Nandas are different events.

questions.stem_md: A family tree drawn by students of an imagined class shows three generations of Mauryan rulers. Which ruler stands in the middle, being the son of Chandragupta and the father of Ashoka?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Bindusara. Bindusara ruled between Chandragupta and Ashoka. Seleucus was a Greek ruler, Kautilya a minister, and Mahendra is traditionally named as a son of Ashoka.

questions.stem_md: A museum label at the imagined Anandpur Heritage Centre gives Ashoka's reign as about 268 to 232 BCE. About how many years did he rule?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** About 36 years. Years before the common era count downwards, so 268 minus 232 gives about 36 years. The other options come from adding, miscounting or dropping a digit.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chandragupta Maurya is regarded as the founder of the Mauryan Empire.

**Reason (R):** Megasthenes came to Pataliputra as an envoy of Seleucus Nikator.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but the visit of Megasthenes does not explain why Chandragupta is called the founder; that rests on his overthrow of the Nandas and the building of the empire.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The conflict between Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus Nikator ended with a treaty.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The war of about 305 to 303 BCE was settled by a treaty, after which Megasthenes came to Pataliputra.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these rulers in chronological order, earliest first.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). The Nandas, then Chandragupta, Bindusara and Ashoka.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two achievements of Chandragupta Maurya.
questions.solution_md: Overthrew the Nandas; treaty with Seleucus.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He **overthrew the Nandas** and founded the Mauryan Empire in about 321 BCE.
2. He **defeated Seleucus Nikator** in the north-west and made a **treaty** with him, after which Megasthenes came as envoy.

marking_scheme.step: Overthrew the Nandas, founded the empire

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says the treaty with Seleucus Nikator was a sign of weakness. Give two points showing how the settlement helped Chandragupta Maurya.
questions.solution_md: Secure frontier; recognition abroad.

answer.model_answer_md: The treaty ended the war on the **north-western frontier** and left the empire **secure** in that region. It also brought a **Greek envoy**, Megasthenes, to Pataliputra, so Mauryan power was **recognised abroad**.

questions.stem_md: Name the three major Mauryan rulers in order and give the approximate reign of each.
questions.solution_md: Three rulers with reigns.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Chandragupta Maurya**, about 321 to 297 BCE, the founder of the empire.
2. **Bindusara**, about 297 to 273 BCE, the son of Chandragupta, who held the empire together.
3. **Ashoka**, about 268 to 232 BCE, the grandson of Chandragupta. Dates are approximate and vary between books.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined role-play of the Mauryan court, one student plays the king. Which description of his position best fits the Mauryan system?

options.text_md: He had no officials and decided every village matter himself
He was chosen every year by the people of Pataliputra
He was at the centre of the government and was helped by a council of ministers and many officials
He was only a priest with no control over the army

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He was at the centre of the government and was helped by a council of ministers and many officials. The king stood at the centre of a large administration of ministers and officials. He did not do everything alone, was not chosen yearly, and controlled the army.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined office chart at a school exhibition, a card reads: "I am in charge of collecting the revenue of the empire." Which Mauryan official does the card represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The samaharta. The samaharta was the chief revenue official, while the sannidhata kept the treasury. A kumara was a prince who governed a province, and a mantri was a minister.

questions.stem_md: An imagined heritage trail says: "At Ujjain, a royal prince governed on behalf of the emperor." Which title is commonly taught for such a provincial governor?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Kumara. Provinces were commonly ruled by princes called kumaras. A samaharta handled revenue, a gramani headed a village in the Vedic age, and Dhamma-mahamattas were officers of Ashoka's Dhamma.

questions.stem_md: An imagined traveller writes that Pataliputra was run by a board of thirty members divided into equal committees of five. How many committees did the board have?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Six. Thirty members in committees of five make six committees. Five is the size of each committee, and three and ten do not divide thirty into groups of five.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined debate asks why the Mauryas could govern an empire stretching across much of the subcontinent. Which answer is the strongest?

options.text_md: Every village chose its own ruler without reference to the king
A network of officials from the king down to provinces, districts and villages, with revenue, an army and spies to keep him informed
The empire had no army and no officials
The king stayed in one village and sent no orders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A network of officials from the king down to provinces, districts and villages, with revenue, an army and spies to keep him informed. Layers of officials, a revenue system, an army and spies allowed orders and information to travel. The other options describe rule without a central system.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Mauryan administration is often described as highly organised.

**Reason (R):** It had the king at the centre, a council of ministers, officials for revenue and the treasury, governors for provinces and a board for the capital.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. The layers of officials listed in the reason are exactly what make the administration organised.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these levels of Mauryan government from the centre outwards.

options.text_md: The king and council of ministers

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). King and ministers, province, district, village.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each term of Mauryan administration with its meaning.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Mantriparishad is the council of ministers, samaharta the revenue official, sannidhata the treasury keeper, and kumara a provincial prince.

questions.stem_md: Describe the position of the king and the work of the ministers in the central administration of the Mauryas.
questions.solution_md: King at the centre; ministers and officials.

answer.model_answer_md: The **king** stood at the **centre** of the government and had the final authority. A **council of ministers (mantriparishad)** advised him, and officials such as the **samaharta** and **sannidhata** carried out the work of revenue and treasury.

marking_scheme.step: King at the centre with authority

questions.stem_md: How were the provinces of the Mauryan Empire governed? Name two provincial capitals.
questions.solution_md: Princes; two capitals.

answer.model_answer_md: Provinces were commonly governed by **princes called kumaras**, on behalf of the emperor, and were divided into **districts and villages**. Capitals included **Taxila**, **Ujjain**, **Tosali** and **Suvarnagiri**.

marking_scheme.step: Provinces under kumaras; districts and villages

questions.stem_md: An imagined traveller says the capital, Pataliputra, had a board of thirty members. Describe the board and state two matters its committees looked after, as reported from Megasthenes.
questions.solution_md: Board of thirty; two matters.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The city was run by a **board of thirty members** in **six committees of five**.
2. One committee looked after **crafts and trade**.
3. Another looked after matters such as **foreigners** or **births and deaths**. This account comes from the report of **Megasthenes** and is paraphrased.

marking_scheme.step: Board of thirty, six committees of five

questions.stem_md: Explain, in three points, how the Mauryas kept control of so large an empire.
questions.solution_md: Ministers and officials; provinces; spies and army.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **council of ministers** and officials such as the **samaharta** ran revenue and the treasury.
2. **Provinces** under princes were divided into **districts and villages**, passing orders downwards.
3. **Spies** reported on officials and a large **army** protected the empire.

questions.stem_md:
Four main sources help us to study the Mauryan Empire.

(i) Name the four sources. **[3]**
(ii) Who wrote the Arthashastra and the Indika, and what does each tell us? **[3]**
(iii) Explain why the Ashokan Edicts and the Sanchi Stupa are important. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Four sources; authors and uses; importance of edicts and Sanchi.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The four sources are the **Arthashastra**, the **Indika**, the **Ashokan Edicts** and the **Sanchi Stupa**.

(ii) The **Arthashastra** is attributed to **Kautilya** (Chanakya), minister of Chandragupta, and tells us how a state was expected to be governed. The **Indika** was written by **Megasthenes**, a Greek envoy, and describes Pataliputra and the court as a foreigner saw them.

(iii) The **edicts** were issued by Ashoka himself, carved on rocks and pillars, and record his **Dhamma**, the **Kalinga War** and welfare measures in his own words. The **Sanchi Stupa**, begun under Ashoka and enlarged later, shows **Buddhist art and belief** through its carved gateways.

questions.stem_md:
The Mauryan Empire was built and ruled by three major kings.

(i) List the three kings in order with approximate reigns. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the achievements of Chandragupta Maurya. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why Ashoka is remembered more than the other two rulers. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Rulers with reigns; achievements of Chandragupta; why Ashoka is remembered.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Chandragupta Maurya**, about 321 to 297 BCE; **Bindusara**, about 297 to 273 BCE; **Ashoka**, about 268 to 232 BCE. Dates vary between books.

(ii) Chandragupta **overthrew the Nandas** and founded the empire. He fought **Seleucus Nikator** in the north-west and made a **treaty** with him, and the envoy **Megasthenes** came to Pataliputra.

(iii) Ashoka is remembered for the **Kalinga War** and his turn to **Dhamma**. He issued **edicts** that survive in stone, set up **pillars** and **stupas**, supported **Buddhism** and organised **welfare**. Because his own words survive, we know more about him than about his predecessors.

questions.stem_md:
The Mauryas governed their empire through a well-organised administration.

(i) Describe the position of the king and the council of ministers. **[3]**
(ii) How were the provinces and districts governed? **[3]**
(iii) Describe the administration of Pataliputra, and say how spies and the army helped the king. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: King and ministers; provinces and districts; Pataliputra, spies and army.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **king** was at the **centre** of the government with the final authority. A **council of ministers (mantriparishad)** advised him, and officials such as the **samaharta** (revenue) and the **sannidhata** (treasury) carried out the work.

(ii) **Provinces** were governed by **princes called kumaras**, with capitals such as **Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali** and **Suvarnagiri**. Provinces were divided into **districts and villages**, so orders reached the countryside.

(iii) As reported from Megasthenes, **Pataliputra** was run by a **board of thirty** in **six committees of five**, looking after matters such as crafts, trade and foreigners. **Spies** reported to the king on officials and enemies, and a large **army** defended the empire and kept order.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Board of thirty in six committees

questions.stem_md:

questions.solution_md: Kalinga and its effect; three principles; moral code and the Dhamma-mahamattas.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The war was fought in about **261 BCE**. The edicts describe the great **suffering** it caused and Ashoka's **remorse**, after which he turned away from conquest by war.

(ii) Three principles were **tolerance of all sects**, **non-violence** and **respect for elders and teachers**. Kindness to servants and the welfare of people and animals were also taught.

(iii) Dhamma set out **common conduct** that people of every faith could follow and did not ask anyone to give up their own beliefs, so many historians call it a **moral code**, not a separate religion. Ashoka appointed **Dhamma-mahamattas** who travelled among the people, explained right conduct and looked after the welfare of all sects.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) A moral code, not a new religion

questions.stem_md:
An imagined class prepares a wall display on Ashoka's Dhamma.

(i) What was Dhamma, and which event led Ashoka to adopt it? **[3]**
(ii) Give four principles of Dhamma, with an everyday example of any one. **[3]**
(iii) The display says, "Dhamma was only a personal belief of the king." Explain why this is incomplete, with two points. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: What Dhamma was and why adopted; four principles and an example; why the display is incomplete.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Dhamma** was a code of **right conduct**, not a separate religion according to most historians. The **Kalinga War** of about 261 BCE and the sorrow it caused led Ashoka to adopt it.

(ii) Four principles were **tolerance**, **non-violence**, **respect for elders and teachers** and **kindness to servants**. For example, a student who listens respectfully to a teacher shows respect for teachers.

(iii) The statement is incomplete because Ashoka made Dhamma a **policy of the state**: he appointed **Dhamma-mahamattas** to spread it and look after welfare, and he had it announced in **edicts** carved on rocks and pillars across his empire. It was therefore a public policy as well as a personal conviction.

questions.stem_md:
Ashoka's Dhamma had effects on the empire and beyond.

(i) Describe its effects on administration and on the welfare of the people. **[3]**
(ii) Explain its effects on the spread of Buddhism and on culture. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate: some historians say Dhamma weakened the empire, but others disagree. Present both views. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Administration and welfare; Buddhism and culture; two views on decline.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Dhamma-mahamattas** were appointed, officials were asked to treat the people fairly, and **welfare** measures such as shaded roads, wells, rest-houses and care for animals were undertaken.

(ii) Royal support, the **Third Buddhist Council** at Pataliputra and **missions** such as that of **Mahendra and Sanghamitra** to Sri Lanka helped **Buddhism** to spread. **Stupas** such as Sanchi, **pillars** such as the Lion Capital of Sarnath (the basis of India's national emblem) and the **edicts** left a lasting mark on culture.

(iii) Some historians argue that stressing Dhamma and non-violence reduced the **military strength** of the empire. Others point to **weak successors**, the **size** of the empire and **financial strain** as the main causes. Because the evidence is limited, the question remains **debated**.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) The other view and why debated

questions.stem_md:
A student in an imagined debate says: "We should trust the edicts more than any other source, because the king himself spoke in them."

(i) Name two other sources of Mauryan history besides the edicts. **[3]**
(ii) State two things the edicts tell us about Ashoka. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the student's view: how far is it fair, and how should a historian use the edicts? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Other sources; what edicts tell; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Two other sources are the **Arthashastra** (attributed to Kautilya) and the **Indika** (Megasthenes); the **Sanchi Stupa** is a third.

(ii) The edicts tell us of the **Kalinga War** and Ashoka's **remorse**, and of his **Dhamma**, with its principles and welfare measures.

(iii) The view is **partly fair**: the edicts are **direct** and carved in stone, so they preserve his words and were not changed by later writers. But they are **royal messages**, so they present the king's own aims and say little about ordinary lives, the army or the empire's weaknesses. A historian therefore reads them **together with** other sources, such as the Indika and the Arthashastra, and notes what each can and cannot show.
